title: Profiling and Benchmarking
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of profiling and benchmarking and identify its main inputs, outputs or constraints.
Apply measuring runtime in a minimal example and state the expected result before checking it.
Test one relevant edge, missing or failure case and describe a limitation of the result.

content.intro: Profiling and Benchmarking is part of Advanced R Programming and Performance. Start with measuring runtime and connect it to the worked example and expected result.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: Profiling and Benchmarking is one step in Advanced R Programming and Performance; advanced behavior is best understood by observing semantics and measuring bottlenecks, not guessing. The example is intentionally small so you can predict its result before checking it in a local R session.

items.title: Measuring Runtime
items.text: For measuring runtime, parse values to a date-time class first and verify formats, timezone assumptions and a boundary date.

items.text: For system.time(), parse values to a date-time class first and verify formats, timezone assumptions and a boundary date.

items.title: Benchmarking Alternatives
items.text: Compare benchmarking alternatives using concrete trade-offs, assumptions and maintenance needs; state when each choice is appropriate.

items.title: Sampling-Based Profiling
items.text: For sampling-based profiling, state the statistical question and assumptions first, then describe the estimate or diagnostic in context.

items.title: Using Rprof() and Profiling Tools
items.text: Build the smallest example for using rprof() and profiling tools, inspect the returned object, and confirm its names, type and shape before using it downstream.

items.title: Identifying Actual Bottlenecks
items.text: Explain identifying actual bottlenecks in the context of profiling and benchmarking, connect it to the example, and verify one expected result or edge case.

content_blocks.title: Work through it
content_blocks.text: Prefer clarity first; profile representative data before optimizing and verify optimized results against a reference. Change one input or condition at a time, compare the observed result with your prediction, and write down one limitation.

content_blocks.title: R example: Profiling and Benchmarking
content_blocks.expected_output: A timing object is printed with elapsed/user/system time fields; values vary by machine.
content_blocks.run_instructions: CodeLeaf does not provide an R runtime. This block is an inspectable reference example; execute it in a local R console or a reviewed R-aware environment. Static validation checks file structure, not R semantics.
content_blocks.reset_steps: No example is executed by this CodeLeaf lesson. For a local run, use synthetic data in a temporary working directory, avoid production credentials or destructive writes, and restart a clean R session to clear lesson objects.
content_blocks.limitations: Benchmark representative workloads and compare equivalent outputs before optimizing. Verify the snippet and expected output with the supported R and package versions before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Common pitfall
content_blocks.text: Do not treat a syntactically plausible example as proof of correctness. For profiling and benchmarking, check the input type, missing/empty cases, output shape, and domain assumptions.

content.task: Apply profiling and benchmarking to a small synthetic example. Start with measuring runtime, predict the result, compare it with a local R run, test one edge or failure case, and document one limitation. For integrations or package-dependent topics, submit a safe verification plan rather than claiming the code ran.

State the expected result before running the example.
Verify one relevant boundary, missing-value or failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example without checking its inputs or output shape.
common_mistakes.why: R can coerce types, propagate missing values or simplify results unexpectedly.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect with str(), class(), typeof(), length() or dim() and add a direct check.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a demonstration as proof that every edge case works.
common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing values, dependencies and version differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Test a normal case and a boundary/failure case in a clean local R session.

common_mistakes.why: The conclusion depends on data provenance, transformations and assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Record input source, cleaning choices and known limitations beside the result.
